Faculty of Mechanical Engineering
Vidi grants awarded to two Mechanical Engineering scientists
Laura Ferranti and Davood Farhadi have both received a Vidi grant from funding body NWO. With funding of up to €850,000 each, they will pursue ambitious robotics research projects from very different perspectives. Ferranti aims to make robots safer and more trustworthy when working alongside people, while Farhadi is developing elastic robots that can think and act without electronics.
New metamaterial design recreates one of nature's toughest connections
Bone and tendon could hardly be more different. One is hard and rigid, the other soft and flexible. Yet in the human body they are connected by a remarkably strong interface that rarely fails. For decades, scientists have struggled to recreate this natural transition. Now, a TU Delft team has taken a major step forward. By providing new strategies to combine two types of metamaterials, they have engineered structures that closely mimic the bone-tendon interface. The work was published in Nature Communications.
TU Delft launches new bachelor programme in Health and Technology
High school students making decisions about higher education will have a new option to consider this autumn. The BSc Health and Technology is a new TU Delft undergraduate programme which will educate graduates capable of designing and integrating the smart solutions and innovations needed to accelerate the healthcare transition.
New Biolab advances mechanical engineering approach to health research
The Faculty of Mechanical Engineering at TU Delft has opened a new state-of-the-art biological laboratory that brings together biosample preparation, advanced imaging and mechanical testing in a single facility. The unique research environment enables scientists to culture living cells, observe them in real time and perform direct mechanical characterization on biological samples. The new facility strengthens the faculty’s growing focus on health-related research and supports its ambition to apply a mechanical engineering perspective to biomedical challenges.
Untangling the meta-biomaterial puzzle one property at a time | TU Delft
TU Delft scientists have now developed a method to decouple properties of metamaterials. Their work, published in Nature Communications, helps to understand how individual material properties influence cell behaviour and could accelerate the development of next-generation biomaterials.
ERC Starting Grant to unravel how heart tissue behaves and adapts
Associate professor Mathias Peirlinck of TU Delft has been awarded a European Research Council (ERC) Starting Grant. With the €1.5 million grant, he will investigate the mechanics of heart muscle tissue. His goal is not only to understand how cardiac tissue responds to mechanical forces, but also how it adapts over time to changing loads. By developing new computational methods, he aims to infer from experimental measurements which processes drive this behaviour. A better understanding of these mechanisms could ultimately contribute to improved treatment strategies for heart failure.
Gabe Weymouth is Educator of the Year 2025-2026
For the past three years, Gabe Weymouth has been inspiring TU Delft’s Maritime Engineering students with his enthusiasm, creativity, and engaging teaching style. This year, students recognised his efforts by naming him Teacher of the Year.
Veni grants awarded to four ME researchers
This year, 15 researchers from TU Delft have been awarded a Veni grant by the Dutch Research Council (NWO). Among them are three researchers from the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering (ME): Emma Hinderink, Olger Siebinga, Emanuele Zanetti and Haluk Akay. The grants will support their research projects on how proteins influence droplet formation in food products, the role of implicit communication in interactions between robots and pedestrians, exploring the operational limits of a novel heat pump concept and learning architecture for understanding engineering design. Emma hinderink Understanding oil droplets for more sustainable food production “Many food products contain small oil droplets dispersed in water, known as emulsions. Examples include sauces, dairy products and plant based alternatives,” explains Assistant Professor Emma Hinderink. Proteins are added to form these droplets and play a crucial role by adsorbing at the oil-water interface, thereby enabling the formation of stable droplets. However, how quickly and how effectively proteins adsorb during processing is still not well understood. “In this research project, I will investigate how proteins behave during production and how they influence droplet formation. The results will help us better predict the functional properties of emerging protein sources and enable the rational design of more sustainable food products.” Olger Siebinga Social navigation for mobile robots Mobile robots are increasingly being deployed to support skilled workers in critical sectors. However, these robots struggle to navigate among people because they neither understand nor display the subtle, implicit signals that guide pedestrian interactions, such as shoulder orientation. “We have previously developed a behavioural framework that describes how people use implicit communication during pedestrian interactions,” says postdoctoral researcher Olger Siebinga. “However, robot optimisation software cannot directly use this framework because it does not satisfy the assumptions on which that software is based.” With this project, Siebinga aims to develop new methods that enable robots to incorporate human communication and behavioural models into their navigation. “This will allow robots to move more safely and naturally around people, making them more effective in supporting workers in their daily tasks.” Emanuele Zanetti Exploring a novel heat pump concept Electrification will play a crucial role in the transition towards a carbon neutral society. “One of the major bottlenecks in this transition is the electricity driven generation of high temperature heat,” explains Assistant Professor Emanuele Zanetti. While heat pumps are theoretically highly efficient, their deployment at high temperatures is limited by the extreme operating conditions of compressors. “This research aims to exploit pressure exchange in high temperature heat pumps, which employs a liquid pumped loop to achieve efficient and controlled compression of steam refrigerant via pressure exchange.” By addressing these challenges, the proposed concept can support the industrial deployment of high temperature heat pumps. Haluk Akay Learning architecture for understanding engineering design “AI has transformed many fields, but engineering design presents a unique challenge that standard models cannot yet solve,” explains assistant professor Haluk Akay. Current AI often suggests parts that look right but are physically impossible to build because models lack an understanding of real-world constraints. Akay: “This project introduces DeepDesign, a new learning architecture specifically built to learn the narrow landscape of feasible designs.” By embedding the sequential, hierarchical, and iterative process of design directly into the model’s structure, DeepDesign ensures that AI-generated solutions are functional and manufacturable. “This allows industry to harness vast examples of prior work archives to create better and more sustainable products,” he says. Tools to improve life
The Faculty of Mechanical Engineering develops and uses fundamental knowledge to design tools that give people new possibilities. To make life better, healthier and more sustainable.
Because of our considerable size and versatility, we can combine expertise and make unique connections. In this way, we offer solutions to both small and large societal challenges, in the fields of Health, Transport & Mobility, Energy and High Tech.
